video_title: Dan Ives on Jensen Huang, Nvidia, SpaceX, Tesla, and Blue Wave
gist: Dan Ives (Yorkville Ives) puts ~15% odds on Jensen Huang losing the Nvidia CEO role over the China spying allegations, warning his exit would mean a 25-30% first-day drop and a narrower US-China AI gap. He argues the post-midterm 'blue tidal wave' pulls AI capex peak into 2027 rather than killing it, favoring hyperscalers, Palantir, Meta and Nebius over leveraged neoclouds (CoreWeave) and Oracle, calls Anthropic's IPO repricing to ~$1T healthy, and sees a political discount on SpaceX tied to Texas.

themes.theme: Jensen Huang key-man risk at Nvidia

insights.claim: Dan Ives assigns roughly a 15% probability that Jensen Huang is no longer Nvidia CEO in 12 months and believes the market is pricing a similar ~15% chance.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Market is pricing Jensen staying; any adverse news flow (congressional hearings, board probe) would reprice a large residual risk.
insights.quote: I mean, we assign about 15% chance.

insights.claim: Ives estimates Nvidia stock would fall 25-30% on the first trade if Jensen Huang's departure were announced, implying roughly a $1 trillion shareholder loss on a ~$4.5 trillion company.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Sizes the tail risk for NVDA holders and for hedging via puts/collars around investigation milestones.
insights.quote: I believe first trade stocks down 25 30%.

insights.claim: Prediction market Kalshi assigns about 39% odds Jensen Huang is out by January 1, 2028, 48% by end of 2028, and nearly 60% by January 1, 2031 — far higher than Ives' 15% 12-month estimate.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Gap between prediction-market odds and equity pricing is a watchable sentiment indicator for NVDA tail risk.

insights.claim: The decisive factor for Jensen Huang's survival is whether he lied to the Nvidia board if asked about the matter roughly six months earlier; if he did, Ives says he is out regardless of stature.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Watch the board investigation and congressional findings specifically for disclosure-to-board issues as the trigger event.

insights.claim: Nvidia has no real succession plan: around 60 people report directly to Jensen Huang, so an interim CEO such as CFO Colette Kress could not replicate his role orchestrating the AI ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Key-man risk at Nvidia is structural, so a leadership change would permanently change the company's direction, not just its multiple.
insights.quote: they don't have a succession plan

insights.claim: Ives argues Jensen Huang single-handedly built the AI financing ecosystem (neoclouds, Anthropic, OpenAI, the so-called circular financing), so his exit would ripple to Oracle, neoclouds and Anthropic, not just Nvidia.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Nvidia leadership risk is a correlated risk across the AI-infrastructure complex; position sizing should treat these as one bet.

insights.claim: Other semiconductor stocks have rallied on the Jensen Huang situation because a damaged Nvidia leadership is seen as bullish for competitors such as AMD and Broadcom, and potentially Alphabet.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Pair-trade angle: long AMD/AVGO vs NVDA on escalation of the Jensen investigation.
insights.quote: a damaged Jensen is bullish for AMD like is it bullish for Broadcom?

insights.claim: Even if the Nvidia board clears Jensen Huang, his credibility as the industry's 'gold standard' ambassador is permanently damaged, and a board-only clearance may be seen by investors as a check-the-box exercise from a Jensen-friendly board.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A clean outcome may not fully restore NVDA's premium; independent congressional findings matter more than the board's.

insights.claim: The woman at the center of the allegations worked for a company already on the US government's suspicion list for routing chips to China, which is why Commerce/State focus is intense and the case is complex.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Ties the scandal to export-control enforcement, raising regulatory risk for chip sales channels in Asia (e.g. Singapore).

themes.theme: US-China AI lead and chip exports

insights.claim: Ives believes US chip sales to China are finished, as the Jensen spying story landing a week after the anti-AI 'blue tidal wave' election unites both parties around an anti-China stance.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Remove China revenue from Nvidia/semis models; Chinese domestic chipmakers like Huawei become structurally stronger.
insights.quote: chips going to China that's no like that's done in my view

insights.claim: Ives says for the first time in 30 years the US is ahead of China in tech, and the only two things that could compress that lead — anti-AI politicians and losing Jensen Huang/Nvidia — both partially happened in the same week.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Geopolitical AI-race risk premium has risen; watch for sudden Chinese frontier-model or chip breakthroughs over the next 6-12 months.
insights.quote: for the first time in 30 years US is ahead of China when it comes tech

insights.claim: If information was actually obtained from Jensen Huang, the impact might only surface 6-12 months later as an unexpected Chinese breakthrough in frontier models or chips.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A surprise Chinese AI breakthrough would be a 'DeepSeek-style' shock risk for US AI multiples.

themes.theme: Blue tidal wave and the capex cycle

insights.claim: Ives says about 75% of the 800-1,000 planned US data centers are already permitted for the next two years; he expects ~10% (worst case ~20%) won't get built after the blue wave, but demand still exceeds supply 4-to-1.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: The market's 'no more data centers' fear is overdone; the near-term build pipeline is largely locked in.
insights.quote: But demand to supply is still 4 to one.

insights.claim: Ives argues the blue tidal wave pulls the AI capex peak into 2027 instead of 2029, which is actually positive because it eases overbuild fears and lets free cash flow rebound sooner.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Earlier capex peak favors FCF-rich big tech over capex-dependent suppliers and leveraged builders.
insights.quote: So capex peaks you could argue is a positive because it worries about overbuild

insights.claim: Hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon and Meta should be worth more, not less, after the midterms because their existing data-center capacity becomes scarcer and more valuable if new builds are restricted.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Buy-the-dip case on hyperscalers selling off on anti-data-center politics.
insights.quote: So in theory, like hypers scalers post midterms should be up, not down.

insights.claim: Ives compares last week's tech selloff (Nasdaq down 5% in a week, more than 10% from highs) to the panic of 2008, March 2020 and April 2025 Liberation Day, and views it as oversold.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Capitulation-type selling plus growing earnings sets up a contrarian entry in AI leaders.

insights.claim: Pompliano notes the AI bull market is facing hot inflation, rising rates with the 10-year near 5%, oil volatility, a Middle East war and the Nvidia scandal; if stocks rally through it, it would be among the most resilient bull markets ever.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: The list of macro headwinds is largely known; resilience through them would be a strong bullish tell.
insights.quote: It's like you're throwing the kitchen sink at this bull market trying to stop it.

insights.claim: Ives still expects tech stocks to rise 20-25% next year, with $3-4 trillion of AI spending making the cycle more elongated and separating winners from losers rather than ending it.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Stay long AI but rotate toward the best-positioned names: Apple, hyperscalers, Palantir.
insights.quote: tech stocks that are up 20 25% next year

insights.claim: Big tech companies that tell communities they will cut 50% of white-collar jobs while electric bills rise will face local opposition to data centers, whereas Meta has worked with communities on its buildout.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Community relations and power costs are becoming a differentiating factor in who can keep building capacity.

insights.claim: Anthropic's proposed IPO valuation fell from rumored $2 trillion three weeks ago to $1.5 trillion to about $1 trillion as its roadshow launched, a ~50% cut that Ives calls healthy.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A digestible IPO price lowers the risk of a broken deal that would have hurt AI sentiment broadly.
insights.quote: I think it's healthy.

insights.claim: Ives says justifying a $1.5 trillion Anthropic valuation would require roughly $600-800 billion of annual revenue within six to seven years.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Useful benchmark for judging the Anthropic IPO multiple versus realistic growth.

insights.claim: Ives predicts OpenAI will go public around late winter or spring 2027, benefiting from going second by learning price discovery from Anthropic's IPO, and that it is building its enterprise business differently.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Anthropic's after-market performance will set the bar for an OpenAI listing in 2027.
insights.quote: probably like by spring 27 you maybe late winter open AI goes public

insights.claim: Pompliano argues companies building on frontier models face platform risk because the model provider sees their usage data and can launch competing products, as with Anthropic's new personal finance tool; partner CEOs privately agreed.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Application-layer companies dependent on one frontier lab carry vendor-turned-competitor risk; favors sovereign/private AI stacks.
insights.quote: your vendor could become your competitor

insights.claim: Ives frames enterprise AI adoption in three phases: rush to partner with frontier labs to 'get in the game', then wall off data and pursue sovereign AI, then increasingly run AI independently — partly driven by spending caps.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Over 12-18 months, enterprise spend may shift from frontier-model APIs toward data-control and sovereign AI vendors.

insights.claim: Ives calls Oracle the poster child for excessive AI leverage — it built itself into a hyperscaler on the back of a ~$300 billion OpenAI deal while cutting into the organization's bone and muscle — and remains cautious on the stock.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Oracle is the most exposed large-cap to an earlier capex peak and tighter credit.
insights.quote: it's the reason we've been more cautious on Oracle

insights.claim: Ives says CoreWeave is not in a good spot because of its debt load and structure as essentially an SPV for Nvidia; he thinks it survives but its capital structure must change, while Nebius is disproportionately better positioned.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Within neoclouds, prefer Nebius over CoreWeave; watch for CoreWeave recapitalization or dilution.
insights.quote: I still believe it's like a survivor but they their capital structure needs to change

insights.claim: Ives expects some neoclouds to lose the game of musical chairs as cost and scarcity of capital bite, with the market wrongly pricing in no new data centers by 2028.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Expect consolidation/failures among smaller GPU-cloud providers.

insights.claim: Palantir looks increasingly well positioned because Alex Karp's early push into sovereign AI and use cases fits the shift from picks-and-shovels to applications, alongside Snowflake, Salesforce and ServiceNow.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Rotate within AI from infrastructure toward applied-AI software leaders.

insights.claim: Marvell's stock-for-stock merger of over $100 billion sold off sharply because it raises execution risk; Ives questions whether the deal ultimately happens given the violent negative reaction.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Deal-break risk is a live catalyst for Marvell shares.

themes.theme: Musk, SpaceX, Tesla and Texas politics

insights.claim: Ives estimates SpaceX trades at a roughly 20-25% political discount after the midterms because its data-center buildout depends on Texas, where a newly elected governor creates friction; resolving it would be significant for the stock.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A Musk-Texas accommodation is a re-rating catalyst for SpaceX (down ~13-14% over the past month).
insights.quote: I think there's like a 20 25% discount right now in SpaceX

insights.claim: Ives still believes SpaceX will acquire Tesla, but the new political environment adds regulatory hurdles to the merger, which is weighing on Tesla's stock.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Merger optionality remains in TSLA but on a longer, less certain timeline.
insights.quote: I still believe SpaceX acquires Tesla.

insights.claim: SpaceX needs to become a hyperscaler, and Ives views orbital data centers as many years out, so the near-term buildout must happen in Texas and Musk will have to offer an olive branch to politicians.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Don't underwrite SpaceX on orbital compute near term; track Texas negotiations instead.

insights.claim: Ives backs Tesla's decision to stop Cybertruck production and redirect capacity to Cybercab, arguing Tesla's future is physical AI: autonomy, robotics and Optimus.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Tesla bull case rests on autonomy/robotics execution, not vehicle volumes.

insights.claim: Ives says China is clearly ahead of the US in robotics outside of Tesla, and expects Chinese firms to sell humanoids first, with US humanoids moving from prototype to functional reality in about two years.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Humanoid commercialization leadership may sit with Chinese players; US humanoid revenue is a ~2027-2028 story.
insights.quote: China is way ahead of the US outside of Tesla at scale

insights.claim: Ives says Meta is in a very strong AI position, underappreciated by its stock, thanks to ~3.6 billion users and available capacity; monetization of its Muse model is key and should let it narrow the gap with Anthropic and OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Meta is Ives' favored mega-cap AI catch-up trade; watch Muse monetization milestones.
insights.quote: Meta is in actually a very strong position. I think that's not reflected in the stock.
